fields.complete_source:
Solution:
Consider a river crossing problem defined by the inputs n, k, and an n-vertex
graph G. There are n passengers to be transported across a river by a pilot, Charon. The
ferry has a maximum capacity of k individuals, which must include Charon to operate the
vessel. The graph G defines conflict constraints: an edge between two vertices indicates
that the corresponding passengers are enemies. The safety conditions dictate that no pair
of enemies may be present together on either riverbank unless Charon is also present at
that location. Prove that the decision problem of determining whether a valid sequence of
crossings exists to transport all n passengers across the river is NP-hard.
NP-hardness of the River Crossing Problem with Conflict
Constraints
We consider the following decision problem:
Instance: a simple undirected graph G = (V, E) with |V | = n, and an integer k ≥1 (boat
capacity, counting the pilot Charon). Initially, Charon and all n passengers are on the left
bank. A move consists of Charon crossing the river with at most k −1 passengers (since the
boat capacity k includes Charon). The safety constraint is:
No pair of enemies (i.e., adjacent vertices in G) may be present together on a
bank unless Charon is also present on that bank.
Question: Is there a sequence of crossings that transports all n passengers to the right bank,
respecting the safety constraint at all times?
We prove:
Theorem 1. The above decision problem is NP-hard.
Proof. We reduce from the NP-complete problem Vertex Cover. Recall: given a graph
G = (V, E) and an integer K, the question is whether G has a vertex cover of size at most
K, i.e., a set S ⊆V with |S| ≤K such that every edge of G has at least one endpoint in
S. Equivalently, S is a vertex cover if and only if V \ S is an independent set (contains no
edge).
We will show that for any graph G and any integer K ≥1, the following equivalence holds:
G has a vertex cover of size ≤K
⇐⇒
the river crossing instance (G, k) with k := K + 1 is feasible.
(1)
This yields a polynomial-time many-one reduction from Vertex Cover to the river crossing
problem (we comment on the K = 0 edge case at the end), proving NP-hardness.
We begin with a simple but crucial observation formalizing the safety rule.
Lemma 1. At any time when Charon is not on a given bank, the set of passengers on that
bank must form an independent set in G. Equivalently, whenever Charon departs a bank, the
set he leaves behind must be independent.
1

Proof. By the safety constraint, no pair of enemies may be present together on a bank without
Charon. This is precisely the definition of an independent set on that bank whenever Charon
is absent. The departing condition is immediate.
We now prove the two directions of (1).
(⇒) Suppose the river crossing instance (G, k) with k = K + 1 is feasible. Consider the
very first trip from the left bank to the right bank. Let S ⊆V be the set of passengers who
board the boat with Charon on this first trip; thus |S| ≤k −1 = K. By Lemma 1, the set of
passengers left behind on the left bank at that moment is V \S, and it must be independent.
Therefore S is a vertex cover of G with |S| ≤K. Hence G has a vertex cover of size at most
K.
(⇐) Conversely, suppose G has a vertex cover S ⊆V with |S| ≤K = k −1. Let I := V \ S,
which is an independent set (by the vertex-cover characterization). We explicitly construct
a safe crossing schedule that moves all passengers to the right bank.
If S = ∅(i.e., E = ∅), the instance is trivial: I = V is independent, and Charon can
shuttle at most k −1 passengers at a time until everyone is on the right bank; when the boat
is away, the left bank contains only an independent set, and the right bank also contains an
independent set when Charon departs it.
Now suppose S ̸= ∅. Fix any vertex j ∈S and let J := {j}. We perform the following
repeating four-move cycle (we write L and R for left and right bank, respectively), ensuring
the safety condition by Lemma 1 at each departure:
• Step 1 (L→R): Charon takes the entire S to the right bank. This is allowed since
|S| ≤k −1. The left bank now contains exactly I, which is independent, so it is safe
while Charon is away.
• Step 2 (R→L): Charon returns to the left bank with S \ J (i.e., leaving J = {j} on
the right bank). This is allowed since |S \ J| = |S| −1 ≤k −2 < k. The set J is
independent, so the right bank is safe when Charon departs.
• Step 3 (L→R): From the left bank, Charon takes back S\J together with one arbitrary
vertex x ∈I that is still on the left bank (if any). Capacity is respected because
|S \ J| + 1 ≤(k −2) + 1 = k −1. After departure, the left bank contains I \ {x} (still
independent), so it is safe. Upon arrival, the right bank temporarily contains S ∪{x}
with Charon present.
• Step 4 (R→L): Charon returns with the entire S to the left bank (again allowed since
|S| ≤k −1), leaving {x} on the right bank. Since {x} ⊆I is independent, the right
bank is safe when Charon departs.
Each four-move cycle moves exactly one vertex x from I to the right bank permanently.
Repeating this cycle |I| times transfers all vertices of I to the right bank, after which the
configuration is: right bank contains all of I, left bank contains all of S with Charon present.
Finally, perform one last trip L→R taking all of S to the right bank (capacity-respecting),
and we are done. At every departure, the bank left behind is independent (either I with one
fewer element, or a singleton {x}), so the safety constraint holds throughout by Lemma 1.
2

Therefore, given any vertex cover S with |S| ≤k −1, there exists a valid sequence of
crossings, proving the feasibility of (G, k).
Combining the two directions yields (1) for all K ≥1. Hence the mapping
(G, K) 7−→(G, k := K + 1)
is a polynomial-time many-one reduction from Vertex Cover to the river crossing decision
problem, establishing NP-hardness.
Remark on the case K = 0: This edge case can be handled separately within the reduction
in a purely polynomial-time manner. If K = 0, then Vertex Cover is a YES-instance iff
E = ∅, which can be checked in polynomial time. If E = ∅, map to any edgeless crossing
instance (e.g., (G, 2)), which is trivially feasible; if E ̸= ∅, map to a fixed infeasible crossing
instance (e.g., a triangle graph with k = 2), which is infeasible because any first move would
leave two adjacent vertices unsupervised on the left bank. Thus the reduction remains total
and polynomial-time.
This completes the proof that the river crossing decision problem with conflict constraints
is NP-hard.
3
fields.explanation: The original star has singleton center cover. With one passenger seat, its nine-state invariant contains the initial state, is closed under every legal safe move, and omits the goal. Both initial and goal states are safe. The new headline includes Mathlib vertex cover and its cardinality and denies Relation.ReflTransGen of the literal ferry transition, so it excludes every finite schedule, not just a search depth. All five state bits are retained from the original witness; moved passengers start on the pilot bank and at most one moves.
fields.flaw: The claimed reduction equivalence: G has a vertex cover of size ≤ K iff the river-crossing instance (G, k=K+1) is feasible.

fields.witness:
K_{1,3} k=2: 32-state search infeasible; K2 one-crossing

Counterexample to the VC⇒crossing direction: take K=1 and G as the star K_{1,3}, with center c and leaves x,y,z. Vertex cover {c} has size 1, so the VC instance is YES. The reduction sets k=2, so Charon can carry at most one passenger. The crossing instance is infeasible: the first trip must carry c, otherwise c is left with a leaf unsupervised. To move a leaf x, Charon can return alone and take x right. Then right has c and x; on returning, Charon must bring either c or x. Bringing x undoes progress; bringing c leaves c with y,z on the left. From there, carrying y or z would leave c with another leaf unsupervised, so the only safe move is carrying c back, returning to the same loop. A brute-force state search over 2*2^4 states verifies no goal state.
